title: Everything is ugly, so go build something that isn't — Raiza Martin, Huxe (ex NotebookLM)

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary:
Martin opens by observing that AI is blurring professional roles—product, engineering, and UX are converging. She describes a multi-layer cake model with chaos at every layer. She argues every product we use today was designed in the pre-AI era and is therefore the ugliest it will ever be, creating consumer unrest between intuitive AI products and janky legacy products. This unrest will drive a rebuilding revolution. Building a real product is a forceful experience requiring personal clarity—clarity of vision, purpose, and taste. She illustrates this with NotebookLM's origin as Tailwind, driven by her personal need to ingest documents and chat with them. She advises starting with the job to be done, not pixels, and warns against AI demo disease.

Martin deepens the discussion of value and trust. The value of a product is a promise to users; trust is oxygen. Products start with a credit of negative one, so first impressions matter enormously. She recommends exposing the model's edges—showing where it is dumb rather than papering over failures—and nailing deterministic things before probabilistic delights. She shares that 90% of NotebookLM's first queries were summarization—a testing behavior—and when it failed, users left forever. After earning trust, products gain the potential to delight. Delight lives in the space between technical capabilities and user expectations; you can push one step past familiar without spooking users. Surface delight through agency, not trickery—users must feel they are steering. She warns against shipping a kitchen sink of model capabilities; instead, ship a clear point of view. Restraint is a new innovation multiplier.

In the conclusion, Martin reinforces that people only have bandwidth for one thing in a product, using Spotify as an example—despite its many features, users just use it to play music. She sees the Huxe product's lack of focus as a form of demo disease. She synthesizes her framework: clarity gives energy for the hard job, purpose keeps focus on the outcome, trust in purpose earns user belief, belief creates the opportunity to delight, delight proves potential, and the kitchen sink serves as a checks-and-balances mechanism keeping the team honest about whether they are meeting the first four principles. That is how you build something that isn't ugly.

sections.title: Introduction: Blending Roles and Invisible Participants
sections.summary: Martin opens by asking the audience what they do, noting that AI is blurring professional boundaries. She describes teams as now augmented with invisible AI participants—every doc, slide, and artifact has a ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini behind it. She frames the current moment as chaotic but full of superpowers.

sections.title: The Ugly Adolescent Phase and Consumer Unrest
sections.summary: Martin argues every product we use is the ugliest it will ever be because it was created in the pre-AI era. She identifies consumer unrest: after using intuitive AI products, users find the rest of the world janky. She predicts a phase where everything gets rebuilt.

sections.title: Chaos and Opportunity: The Role of Product People
sections.summary: Martin acknowledges the chaos and discomfort at every layer—job security is uncertain across roles. She argues opportunity is complementary to chaos and the product person's job is to find the nugget of opportunity and explode it like a popcorn kernel.

sections.title: Personal Clarity: The Force Behind Product Building
sections.summary: Martin describes building a product as a forceful experience requiring personal clarity of vision, purpose, and taste from a singular individual. She shares the NotebookLM origin story—originally Tailwind, announced at Google IO 2023—driven by her personal need as a full-time student and Google employee to ingest documents and chat with them.

sections.title: Start With the Job, Not the Pixels
sections.summary: Martin advises starting with the job to be done, not pixels. Taste is about outcomes, not aesthetics. She warns against AI demo disease and introduces purpose as the north star that helps reject novelty. Users don't care if something is AI—they care about intent delivered inevitably.

sections.title: Value as Promise and Trust as Oxygen
sections.summary: Martin explains that the value of a product is a promise to users and trust is oxygen. Products start with a credit of negative one, so first impressions matter. She recommends exposing the model's edges—showing where it is dumb—rather than papering over failures, because building AI is still a very human process. She stresses nailing deterministic things before delightful probabilistic bits: a good app is still just a good app.

sections.title: The Summarization Testing Behavior and Fragile Trust
sections.summary: Martin shares that 90% of NotebookLM users' first queries were summarization queries—a testing behavior. When it failed, users left forever. She emphasizes that trust is not cheap: if you get a user to try your product, make it as good as possible the first time because they won't come back.

sections.title: Earning the Potential to Delight
sections.summary: After earning trust, products gain the potential to delight. Martin describes delight as living between technical capabilities and user expectations—you can push one step past familiar without spooking users. She advises surfacing delight through agency, not trickery: users must feel they are steering. The NotebookLM podcast feature exemplifies playful, unexpected delight with healthy tension between user and machine.

sections.title: Kitchen Sink Anti-Pattern and Restraint as Innovation Multiplier
sections.summary: Martin warns against shipping a kitchen sink of model capabilities rather than a clear point of view. The barrier to shipping is not capability but judgment. She asks whether products respect user time, data, and agency, and argues restraint is a new innovation multiplier. She shares a Huxe example where an app did everything but she only used one feature, reinforcing the importance of focus and personal clarity.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Framework for Building Something That Isn't Ugly
sections.summary: Martin reinforces that people only have bandwidth for one thing in a product, using Spotify as an example—despite its many features, users just use it to play music. She sees the Huxe product's lack of focus as demo disease. She synthesizes her framework: clarity gives energy for the hard job, purpose keeps focus on the outcome, trust in purpose earns user belief, belief creates the opportunity to delight, delight proves potential, and the kitchen sink serves as a checks-and-balances mechanism keeping the team honest about the first four principles. That is how you build something that isn't ugly.

demonstrations: NotebookLM first version called Tailwind, announced at Google IO 2023, shown as an example of personal clarity driving a skeptical project forward.
NotebookLM auto-summary feature served as both a tutorial and a useful at-a-glance tool, arrived at by obsessively driving at value.
NotebookLM podcast feature as an example of delightfulness—unexpected, funny, playful, with healthy tension between user and machine.
Huxe app that did everything (chat, podcasts, news, images, videos) but Martin only used one feature, illustrating the kitchen sink anti-pattern.
Spotify example: despite being a huge product with many features, people use it for one thing—playing music—illustrating user bandwidth for focus.
limitations: AI products are in a clunky, awkward phase with significant chaos at every layer of the product-building process.
Many AI products suffer from demo disease—looking impressive in demos but not serving real user needs.
When first-time summarization failed in NotebookLM, users left forever, showing how fragile trust is.
Kitchen sink products that try to do everything end up confusing users who don't know when to use each feature.
quantitativeClaims: 90% of NotebookLM users' first queries were summarization queries, functioning as a testing behavior.
Every team now effectively has as many invisible AI participants as human members (e.g., five people and five ChatGPTs).
Most products get a credit of negative one—most users won't even try them.
